Spin-orbit-entangled Jeff=12J_{\rm eff}=\frac{1}{2} magnetism and unconventional spin freezing in the bond-disordered pyrochlore antiferromagnet NaCdCo2F7

Abstract

Bond disorder in frustrated pyrochlore antiferromagnets can give rise to fundamentally different quantum ground states depending on the nature of the local magnetic moments. Here, we show that the bond-disordered Jeff=12J_{\rm eff}=\frac{1}{2} pyrochlore antiferromagnet NaCdCo2F7 realizes an unconventional spin-glass-like state with continued dynamics, in stark contrast to its isostructural S=12S=\frac{1}{2} NaCdCu2F7 counterpart. High-field magnetization and Co L2,3L_{2,3}-edge XAS/XMCD establish spin-orbit-entangled Jeff=12J_{\rm eff}=\frac{1}{2} Co2+ moments with a substantial unquenched orbital contribution, consistent with local X​YXY anisotropy seen in the isostructural NaA′′A^{\prime\prime}Co2F7 (A′′A^{\prime\prime} = Ca, Sr) analogues. μ\muSR and 23Na NMR measurements reveal progressive slowing of spin fluctuations below ∼10\sim 10 K, culminating in a partially frozen state with persistent low-temperature dynamics that deviates from a canonical spin glass. Comparison with the isostructural bond-disordered pyrochlore NaCdCu2F7, which realizes a random-singlet state, reveals a fundamentally different response of spin-orbit-entangled Co2+ moments to bond disorder. These results identify spin-orbit coupling as a key ingredient governing the fate of bond-disordered frustrated pyrochlore magnets.

I Introduction

Geometrically frustrated magnets provide a fertile platform for the study of unconventional magnetic ground states, including spin glasses, spin ices, and spin liquids [49, 21, 5, 48, 34]. Among the most prominent realizations are pyrochlore magnets, in which antiferromagnetically coupled magnetic ions occupy a three-dimensional network of corner-sharing tetrahedra that gives rise to strong geometric frustration, hindering the development of trivial magnetic order. In these systems, subtle differences in electronic configuration, spin-orbit coupling, local crystal-field environment, exchange anisotropy and disorder can stabilize fundamentally different ground states [22, 50].

The rare-earth family of A23+​B24+A^{3+}_{2}B^{4+}_{2}O7 pyrochlore oxides has been extensively studied due to the availability of large single crystals in many cases, enabling detailed microscopic investigations of their rich variety of exotic magnetic ground states [19, 34, 63, 65]. In these materials, spin-orbit coupling and crystal-field effects play a central role in forming strong Ising or XY anisotropy, stabilizing diverse magnetic phases such as spin-ice or unconventional ordered states [61, 54, 12, 71, 64]. However, the weak exchange energy scale of localized 4​f4f rare-earth moments typically confines the relevant magnetic phenomena to extremely low temperatures, making experimental access to their low-energy physics challenging.

Transition-metal fluoride pyrochlores A′⁣+A′′2+B2+2A^{\prime+}A^{\prime\prime 2+}B^{2+}_{2}F7 [24, 50, 35, 37, 36, 55, 32, 33, 31], conversely, host divalent magnetic 3​d3d transition-metal ions on the pyrochlore BB site, leading to substantially stronger superexchange interactions mediated by fluoride ligands. Charge balancing and structure stability constraints, however, require random mixing of monovalent A′⁣+A^{\prime+} and divalent A′′2+A^{\prime\prime 2+} cations on the nonmagnetic pyrochlore AA sublattice [62]. The associated A′⁣+/A′′2+A^{\prime+}/A^{\prime\prime 2+} ionic-size mismatch then introduces local structural distortions, which perturb the BB–F–BB superexchange pathways and thereby generate a spatial distribution of magnetic exchange interactions. We refer to this exchange randomness as magnetic bond disorder. This weak magnetic bond disorder on the pyrochlore lattice is expected to precipitate spin-glass freezing at a temperature that is commensurate with the exchange variation scale kB​Tf=8/3​Δk_{\rm B}T_{f}=\sqrt{8/3}\Delta [57, 3].

Experimental studies of fluoride pyrochlores broadly support this disorder-driven freezing scenario. A vast majority of the NaA′′A^{\prime\prime}B2B_{2}F7 family (A′′A^{\prime\prime} = Ca, Sr, Cd; BB = Co, Ni, Mn, Fe) [35, 37, 36, 55, 32, 33] undergo spin-glass-like freezing at temperatures Tf=2−4T_{f}=2-4 K, substantially lower than their mean-field exchange energy scales (|θCW|∼70−140|\theta_{\rm CW}|\sim 70-140 K). Within the isostructural NaA′′A^{\prime\prime}Co2F7 (A′′A^{\prime\prime} = Ca, Sr, Cd) series, the role of this disorder is further supported by a systematic correlation between the AA-site ionic-size mismatch and the spin-freezing temperature: TfT_{f} increases from 2.4 K for A′′A^{\prime\prime} = Ca to 3.0 K for A′′A^{\prime\prime} = Sr and 4.0 K for A′′A^{\prime\prime} = Cd, while the corresponding ionic-size mismatch increases from approximately 5.2% to 6.6% and 7.0%, respectively [32].

Despite the apparent spin freezing, local probe measurements on the S=1S=1 NaCaNi2F7 revealed persistent low-temperature spin dynamics well below its freezing temperature [10], while inelastic neutron scattering uncovered spin-liquid-like correlations, including a continuum of magnetic scattering with low-energy pinch points [46, 70]. These observations suggest that geometric frustration inhibits complete static freezing and gives rise to unconventional glassy states rather than canonical spin glasses [72, 59]. Here, we use the term “unconventional spin glass” to refer to a partially frozen, dynamically inhomogeneous state in which quasi-static local magnetism coexists with persistent spin fluctuations well below the bulk freezing temperature, in contrast to the predominantly static frozen state of a canonical spin glass. Strikingly, the recently-synthesized S=12S=\frac{1}{2} Heisenberg pyrochlore antiferromagnet NaCdCu2F7 stands out as an important exception that realizes a disorder-driven random-singlet state rather than an unconventional spin glass [31]. It is characterized by power-law scaling of bulk and local-probe thermodynamic quantities, universal scaling collapse, and the absence of global spin freezing. An important question arises about what governs the fundamentally different response of fluoride pyrochlores to comparable bond disorder.

Among fluoride pyrochlores, Co2+ systems are particularly intriguing due to the strong spin-orbit coupling of the high-spin 3​d73d^{7} electronic configuration. Single-ion inelastic neutron scattering (INS) studies of NaCaCo2F7 and NaSrCo2F7 established a well-isolated Jeff=12J_{\rm eff}=\frac{1}{2} Kramers doublet characterized by a strongly anisotropic local XY-type gg tensor and anisotropic exchange interactions [52]. Furthermore, diffuse neutron scattering and magnetic pair distribution function studies revealed the emergence of short-range ordered X​YXY clusters at low temperatures, indicative of highly anisotropic short-range magnetic correlations [53, 18]. Complementary 19F and 23Na NMR measurements further demonstrated persistent low-energy spin fluctuations and unconventional freezing dynamics in NaCaCo2F7 [56]. Together, these observations suggest that spin-orbit-entangled Co2+ moments may respond to bond disorder in a fundamentally different manner from nearly isotropic Heisenberg systems. However, analogous microscopic information remains unavailable for NaCdCo2F7, where the strong neutron absorption of natural Cd precludes detailed neutron-scattering investigations of both the crystal-field level scheme and the nature of short-range magnetic correlations.

In this work, we combine high-field magnetization, Co L2,3L_{2,3}-edge X-ray absorption and magnetic circular dichroism (XAS/XMCD), muon spin relaxation (μ\muSR), and 23Na nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) measurements to investigate the magnetic ground state of NaCdCo2F7. High-field magnetization and XAS/XMCD establish spin-orbit-entangled Co2+ moments with a substantial unquenched orbital contribution, consistent with the local X​YXY anisotropy established in the isostructural NaA′′A^{\prime\prime}Co2F7 (A′′A^{\prime\prime} = Ca, Sr) analogues. Furthermore, μ\muSR and 23Na NMR reveal a progressive slowing down of spin fluctuations into an unconventional partially frozen state with persistent low-temperature dynamics. Comparison with the random-singlet S=12S=\frac{1}{2} Heisenberg pyrochlore antiferromagnet NaCdCu2F7 reveals a fundamentally different response to bond disorder, identifying spin-orbit coupling and magnetic anisotropy as key ingredients governing the fate of bond-disordered pyrochlore antiferromagnets.

II Experimental methods

Single crystals of NaCdCo2F7 were grown in an optical floating zone furnace by pre-melting a stoichiometric mix of precursor binary fluorides in a tubular graphite crucible, then hanging the pre-reacted polycrystalline rod for a standard floating-zone growth in a high-pressure dynamic argon atmosphere. Details of the synthesis process are covered in Ref. [32]. Crystals were then oriented for directional property measurements using an in-house Laue diffractometer.

High-field isothermal magnetization was measured on oriented single crystals of NaCdCo2F7 in the High Magnetic Field Laboratory (Hochfeld-Magnetlabor Dresden, HLD) in the Helmholtz-Zentrum Dresden-Rossendorf (HZDR) in Dresden, Germany, using a pulsed 60 T magnet with a cryostat setup allowing the temperature range T=1.37−100T=1.37-100 K [60]. The magnetic field was applied along the cubic high-symmetry directions [100],[110][100],[110] and [111][111]. Calibration of pulsed field data was carried out by normalization against in-house MPMS and PPMS datasets.

XAS/XMCD spectra were measured on an unoriented single crystal of NaCdCo2F7 at the BL29 BOREAS soft X-ray beamline at the ALBA synchrotron in Cerdanyola del Vallès, Barcelona, Spain [6]. The circularly polarized XAS spectra of the Co2+ L2,3L_{2,3} edge were collected between 765−810765-810 eV at 300 K in the normal incidence geometry, using the total electron yield (TEY) mode. A magnetic field of 6 T was applied along the beam direction, using the vector magnet HECTOR. A statistical average of two octets (C+C-C-C+C-C+C+C-) was collected and used for the analysis. The XMCD signal was then calculated as the difference of the XAS spectra with negative and positive helicity.

ZF and LF-μ\muSR measurements were performed at the ISIS Neutron and Muon Source at the Rutherford Appleton Laboratory in Harwell Oxford, United Kingdom. [15] The MUSR instrument was used, utilising a helium cryostat setup for temperatures between T=1.7−50T=1.7-50 K, allowing applied longitudinal fields between μ0​HLF=0−3000\mu_{0}H_{\rm LF}=0-3000 G. The obtained spectra were analyzed using WiMDA [47] and Mantid [4].

NMR measurements were performed using a phase-coherent pulsed spectrometer with a superconducting NMR magnet. A 4He variable temperature insert (VTI) was utilized between T=1.7−60T=1.7-60 K. A custom-wound excitation coil from silver wire was used. The single crystal of NaCdCo2F7 was inserted into the NMR coil, and the coil was mounted on a sample stage equipped with a two-axis rotation mechanism. A small piece of pure Al foil was mounted next to the single-crystal sample as a field marker, and the applied magnetic field was calibrated using its 27Al NMR signal. Frequency-swept 23Na spectra were collected in a constant field μ0​H=2.21331\mu_{0}H=2.21331 T, with the radio-frequency (r.f.) circuit tuned and matched at each point. Nuclear spin echoes were generated using a standard 90°\degree–180°\degree pulse sequence, with a first-pulse duration of 2 - 3 μ\mus, where the r.f. power for nuclear spin excitation was optimized at each NMR spectral peak. The separation τ\tau between the first and second pulse was typically 20 - 30 μ\mus. Echoes were accumulated and Fourier transformed to obtain the spectra.

III Results

III.1 High-field magnetization

High-field isothermal magnetization M⁡(H)M(H) measured in pulsed fields up to 60 T, applied along the [100] direction at temperatures between 1.37−1001.37-100 K, is shown in Fig. 1(a). No magnetization plateaus or field-induced transitions are observed, in contrast to recent theoretical predictions for ideal disorder-free S=12S=\frac{1}{2} pyrochlore Heisenberg antiferromagnets under magnetic field [43, 58, 23]. Instead, the magnetization increases smoothly with field and exhibits a slow Brillouin-like polarization that does not reach full saturation even at the largest field-to-temperature ratio of μ0​H/T∼44\mu_{0}H/T\sim 44 T K-1 achieved at 60 T and 1.37 K. Previous low-field SQUID magnetization measurements of NaCdCo2F7 [32] revealed strong antiferromagnetic exchange interactions characterized by a Curie-Weiss temperature of θCW=−108​(1)\theta_{\rm CW}=-108(1) K. Using the mean-field relation θCW=2​z​J​(J+1)​𝒥/3​kB\theta_{\rm CW}=2zJ(J+1)\mathcal{J}/3k_{B}, where z=6z=6 is the nearest-neighbor coordination number of the pyrochlore lattice and J=Jeff=12J=J_{\rm eff}=\frac{1}{2}, we estimate an average nearest-neighbor exchange coupling of 𝒥≈−36\mathcal{J}\approx-36 K (≈−3.1\approx-3.1 meV). The strong antiferromagnetic exchange interactions combined with the geometrical frustration of the pyrochlore lattice hinder full magnetic saturation even by 60 T, which in a non-interacting Heisenberg system of spins would be expected by several Tesla [69].

Single-ion inelastic neutron scattering (INS) studies of the isostructural NaA′′A^{\prime\prime}Co2F7 (A′′A^{\prime\prime} = Ca, Sr) family revealed a well-isolated spin-orbit-coupled Jeff=12J_{\rm eff}=\frac{1}{2} Kramers doublet ground state with a strongly X​YXY-like gg tensor (gxy=6.08g_{\rm xy}=6.08 and gz=1.87g_{z}=1.87), separated from the first excited doublet by 28.05(2) and 29.31(2) meV (or 325.5(2) and 340.1(2) K) in A′′A^{\prime\prime} = Ca and Sr, respectively [52]. While neutron scattering studies are not possible in NaCdCo2F7 due to the very large neutron absorption cross-section of natural Cd, the two-level Schottky anomaly fit of magnetic specific heat revealed a possible first excited state at around 33.9(5) meV (or 393(6) K) [32]. Consistently, the magnetic entropy approaches Rln(2) by 70 K in all A′′A^{\prime\prime} = Ca, Sr and Cd cobalt pyrochlores [35, 37, 32], confirming that only the ground-state Jeff=12J_{\rm eff}=\frac{1}{2} Kramers doublet is thermally populated in the temperature range of the present measurements. It is therefore possible to model the low-temperature M⁡(H)M(H) data using a modified Jeff=12J_{\rm eff}=\frac{1}{2} Brillouin function with an effective temperature Teff=T−T0T_{\rm eff}=T-T_{0} accounting for the exchange interactions between Co2+ spins [27, 14]:

M𝐝​(H,T)=M𝐝sat​tanh​(g𝐝​μB​μ0​H2​kB​(T−T0))M_{\mathbf{d}}(H,T)=M_{\mathbf{d}}^{\rm sat}\mathrm{tanh}\left(\frac{g_{\mathbf{d}}\mathrm{\mu_{B}\mu_{0}}H}{2\mathrm{k_{B}}(T-T_{0})}\right) (1)

where M𝐝sat=g𝐝​μB/2M_{\mathbf{d}}^{\rm sat}=g_{\mathbf{d}}\mu_{\rm B}/2 is the saturation moment along the field direction 𝐝=𝐇→/|𝐇→|\mathbf{d}=\vec{\mathbf{H}}/|\vec{\mathbf{H}}|, g𝐝g_{\mathbf{d}} is the projection of the anisotropic single-ion gg-tensor onto the field direction averaged over the four sites on the tetrahedron, and T0T_{0} is a phenomenological mean-field parameter that reflects the strength of antiferromagnetic exchange interactions. The fits are shown in Fig. 1(a) as dashed lines, and the extracted parameters are summarized in Table 1.

A global fit of M⁡(H)M(H) was performed between 1.37−1001.37-100 K along H|[100]H\parallel[100], with the effective gg-factor shared for all temperatures and T0T_{0} fitted independently. The fit yields g[100]=6.563​(1)g_{[100]}=6.563(1), corresponding to a saturation moment of M[100]sat=3.28M_{[100]}^{\rm sat}=3.28 μB\mu_{\rm B}/Co2+. The effective moment evaluated as μeff=g[100]​Jeff​(Jeff+1)​μB=5.68\mu_{\rm eff}=g_{[100]}\sqrt{J_{\rm eff}(J_{\rm eff}+1)}\mu_{\rm B}=5.68 μB\mu_{\rm B}/Co2+ is in good agreement with the orientationally-averaged paramagnetic value of 5.4(1) μB\mu_{\rm B}/Co2+ extracted from the Curie-Weiss analysis of inverse susceptibility [32] between 100−350100-350 K. The phenomenological mean-field interaction parameter T0T_{0} is nearly temperature independent for temperatures between 1.37−50.21.37-50.2 K, with T0[100]≈−121​(3)T_{0}^{[100]}\approx-121(3) K, consistent with the scale of mean-field interactions given by the Curie-Weiss temperature θCW=−108​(1)\theta_{\rm CW}=-108(1) K. The large deviation in the 100 K value, T0[100]T_{0}^{[100]}(100 K) =−151.21​(6)=-151.21(6) K, may be attributed to a non-negligible thermal population of the first excited Kramers doublet.

Using the fitted value g[100]=6.563​(1)g_{[100]}=6.563(1), we can estimate the saturation field from the competition between antiferromagnetic exchange and the Zeeman energy μ0​Hs​a​t=z​|𝒥|2​g​μB​Jeff\mu_{0}H_{\mathrm{s}at}=\frac{z|\mathcal{J}|}{2g\mu_{\rm B}J_{\rm eff}} [39]. For Jeff=12J_{\rm eff}=\frac{1}{2}, z=6z=6, and |𝒥|≈36​K|\mathcal{J}|\approx 36\penalty\ \mathrm{K}, this gives μ0​Hsat∼49​T\mu_{0}H_{\rm sat}\sim 49\penalty\ \mathrm{T}. Instead, only ∼76\sim\!76 % of the expected saturated moment is observed by 60 T at the lowest temperature, as geometrical frustration, quantum fluctuations, and anisotropic exchange interactions all tend to increase the effective saturation field relative to this simple mean-field estimate.

The directional dependence of M⁡(H)M(H) at 4 K is shown in Fig. 1(b) for fields applied along the cubic high-symmetry directions [100][100], [110][110], and [111][111]. For clarity, fits to Equation 1 are shown separately in the inset of Fig. 1(b) due to the large overlap with the experimental data. The magnetization curves appear strongly isotropic, suggesting Heisenberg-like magnetism with only weak signs of anisotropy observed by 60 T, which could come from instrumental effects near the pulsed magnet limit. The extracted parameters for H|[110]H\parallel[110] and [111][111] are essentially identical within the error, with g[110]=g[111]=6.566​(1)g_{[110]}=g_{[111]}=6.566(1) and T0[110]∼T0[111]∼−120T_{0}^{[110]}\sim T_{0}^{[111]}\sim-120 K. In contrast, an independent fit of the 4 K data along the [100] direction yields slightly smaller values of g[100]=6.423​(1)g_{[100]}=6.423(1) and T0[100]=−116.21​(6)T_{0}^{[100]}=-116.21(6) K, as compared to the values extracted from the global fit of the M[100]​(H)M_{[100]}(H) dataset between 1.37−1001.37-100 K. The difference arises largely from the sharing of the gg factor across the whole temperature range, inflating its value while simultaneously influencing the fitted T0T_{0}.

Our results are consistent with the seemingly isotropic high-field magnetization curves of NaCaCo2F7 [69], despite its strongly anisotropic XY-type single-ion gg tensor (OPENgx​y/gz∼3)g_{xy}/g_{z}\sim 3), where one would naively expect |M[100]|<|M[111]|<|M[110]||M_{[100]}|<|M_{[111]}|<|M_{[110]}|. The apparent Heisenberg behavior arises because the local XY anisotropy of each of the four Jeff=12J_{\rm eff}=\frac{1}{2} Co2+ spins on a tetrahedron (each with a local ⟨111⟩\langle 111\rangle anisotropy axis) averages out when projected onto the global field direction, leading to isotropic magnetization curves even in the presence of strong local single-ion anisotropy. The effective projected gg-factor can be calculated from an XY-type anisotropic gg-tensor as geff=13​(2​gx​y2+gz2)g_{\rm eff}=\sqrt{\frac{1}{3}(2g_{xy}^{2}+g_{z}^{2})}, yielding geff=5.08g_{\rm eff}=5.08 for NaCaCo2F7. Our results suggest that NaCdCo2F7 with geff∼6.56g_{\rm eff}\sim 6.56 most likely exhibits a greater local XY-type anisotropy in the form of a larger dominant gx​yg_{xy} component. [29]

III.2 X-ray magnetic circular dichroism

To probe the microscopic origin of the large effective magnetic moment observed in NaCdCo2F7 and related cobalt-based fluoride pyrochlores [32, 35, 37], and in particular the role of spin-orbit coupling (SOC) in the Co2+ magnetic degrees of freedom and its connection to the local magnetic anisotropy established in the isostructural NaA′′A^{\prime\prime}Co2F7 (A′′=A^{\prime\prime}= Ca, Sr) analogues [53, 52], X-ray magnetic circular dichroism (XMCD) measurements were performed at the Co2+ L2,3L_{2,3} absorption edge.

Single-crystal X-ray diffraction studies have shown [32] that Co2+ fully occupies the pyrochlore 16​c16c Wyckoff site with a local D3​dD_{3d} symmetry, coordinated by six fluorine ions forming slightly distorted CoF6 octahedra compressed along the local ⟨111⟩\langle 111\rangle-type (C3C_{3}) axis. This small trigonal compression produces a deviation of the F-Co-F bond angles from the ideal octahedral value of 90°\degree by ±δF−Co−F=8.12​(5)​°\pm\delta_{\rm F-Co-F}=8.12(5)\degree. Such a local symmetry lowering is expected to partially lift the cubic t2​gt_{2g} degeneracy as |t2​g⟩→|a1​g⟩​⨁|egπ⟩\ket{t_{2g}}\rightarrow\ket{a_{1g}}\bigoplus\ket{e_{g}^{\pi}}, while leaving the |eg⟩\ket{e_{g}} orbitals untouched [17]. Together with the strong spin–orbit coupling of high-spin Co2+, this leads to the stabilization of six Kramers doublets, with a Jeff=12J_{\rm eff}=\frac{1}{2} doublet as the ground state [2, 30, 41, 45]. Such spin–orbit-entangled Co2+ moments can exhibit strongly anisotropic local magnetic properties.

The X-ray absorption spectrum (XAS), measured in the TEY mode at T=300T=300 K in an applied field of μ0​H=6\mu_{0}H=6 T, and normalized to the maximum intensity of the L3L_{3} peak, can be seen in Fig. 2(a). The spectrum was corrected by a standard linear background and edge step function subtraction, and is defined as XAS = μ−​(E)+μ+​(E)\mu^{-}(E)+\mu^{+}(E), where μ+​(E)\mu^{+}(E) and μ−​(E)\mu^{-}(E) correspond to the absorption spectra measured using left- and right-circularly polarized X-rays, respectively.

The XAS exhibits the characteristic multiplet structure of octahedrally coordinated high-spin Co2+ (3​d73d^{7}, S=3/2S=3/2), with intense L3L_{3} and L2L_{2} lines centered around 778 eV and 793 eV, respectively. The XMCD spectrum, defined as XMCD = μ−​(E)−μ+​(E)\mu^{-}(E)-\mu^{+}(E), is shown in Fig. 2(b) after normalization to the maximum intensity of the L3L_{3} line. A pronounced negative dichroic signal is observed at the L3L_{3} edge, while the corresponding L2L_{2} contribution is considerably weaker, indicating a sizable unquenched orbital contribution to the Co2+ magnetic moment.

To assess the influence of the small local trigonal distortion on the Co2+ electronic structure, crystal-field multiplet calculations [25, 16] of the Co L2,3L_{2,3} XAS/XMCD spectra were performed using the Crispy [51] interface to Quanty [42]. Two crystal-field models were considered: (i) an ideal octahedral OhO_{h} environment, and (ii) a weakly distorted trigonal environment described within the C3​vC_{3v} point symmetry. Although the true local symmetry of the Co2+ site is D3​dD_{3d}, such a symmetry option is not implemented in Crispy for Co L2,3L_{2,3} calculations. The available C3​vC_{3v} crystal field nevertheless captures the essential trigonal symmetry lowering from cubic symmetry and therefore provides a reasonable approximation for modeling the qualitative effects of trigonal distortion on the XAS/XMCD line shapes.

The dominant octahedral crystal field was parametrized by the cubic splitting parameter 10​D​q=0.910Dq=0.9 eV, which controls the energy separation between the lower t2​gt_{2g} and upper ege_{g} manifolds. Electron-electron interactions were described using uniformly reduced Slater-Condon integrals scaled by factors Fk=0.75F^{k}=0.75 and Gk=0.78G^{k}=0.78 relative to their free-ion Hartree-Fock values. Such reductions are commonly employed in transition-metal multiplet calculations [25, 16] to phenomenologically account for intra-atomic screening and covalency effects, which decrease the effective Coulomb and exchange interactions relative to the ionic limit. Spin–orbit coupling was retained at its atomic value (scale factor ζ=1\zeta=1). To model the experimentally established trigonal distortion of CoF6 octahedra [32], additional trigonal crystal-field parameters DσD_{\sigma} and DτD_{\tau} were introduced within the C3​vC_{3v} crystal-field description [28, 67], which describe the splitting of the cubic |t2​g⟩\ket{t_{2g}} manifold into |a1​g⟩\ket{a_{1g}} and |egπ⟩\ket{e_{g}^{\pi}} states under distortion along the local threefold axis. The influence of the trigonal distortion was investigated by systematically varying DσD_{\sigma} and DτD_{\tau}, as described in the SM [1]. Since these calculations are intended to assess the sensitivity of the calculated spectra to weak trigonal crystal-field perturbations rather than to determine a unique set of crystal-field parameters, the OhO_{h} calculation is retained as the minimal description in the main text. The Hamiltonian parameters used for this OhO_{h} calculation are summarized in Tab. 2.

As shown in Fig. 2(a,b), the OhO_{h} calculation reproduces the overall multiplet structure and the shape of the XMCD line reasonably well, including the dominant negative dichroic response at the L3L_{3} edge characteristic of Co2+ with a substantial orbital contribution. Systematic variations of DσD_{\sigma} and DτD_{\tau} presented in the SM [1] show that the XMCD response is more sensitive to the trigonal crystal field than the XAS line shape. Comparison using normalized residual factors favors a crystal field close to the OhO_{h} limit, although weak trigonal perturbations remain compatible with the experimental spectra. This is consistent with the relatively small structural deviation of the CoF6 octahedra from ideal cubic symmetry reported by single-crystal diffraction studies. The multiplet calculations therefore support the conclusion that the Co2+ electronic structure in NaCdCo2F7 is well described by a predominantly octahedral crystal field, consistent with the expected local Jeff=12J_{\rm eff}=\frac{1}{2} description arising from the interplay of crystal-field splitting and spin-orbit coupling.

Quantitative estimates of the orbital magnetic moment mL=⟨Lz⟩​μBm_{L}=\langle L_{z}\rangle\mu_{\rm B} and the effective spin magnetic moment mSeff=2​⟨Seff⟩​μBm_{S_{\rm eff}}=2\langle S_{\rm eff}\rangle\mu_{\rm B} were obtained using the sum rules analysis [66, 11, 13]. For the Co L2,3L_{2,3} edge, the expectation value of the orbital angular momentum’s projection ⟨Lz⟩\langle L_{z}\rangle is given by

⟨Lz⟩\displaystyle\langle L_{z}\rangle =−43​∫L3+L2XMCD​𝑑E∫L3+L2XAS​𝑑E​(10−⟨n3​d⟩)\displaystyle=-\frac{4}{3}\frac{\int_{L_{3}+L_{2}}\mathrm{XMCD}\penalty\ dE}{\int_{L_{3}+L_{2}}\mathrm{XAS}\penalty\ dE}(10-\langle n_{3d}\rangle)
=−4​q​(10−⟨n3​d⟩)3​r,\displaystyle=-\frac{4q(10-\langle n_{3d}\rangle)}{3r}, (2)

where qq is the integrated XMCD signal over the L3+L2L_{3}+L_{2} edges, rr is the integrated XAS intensity and ⟨n3​d⟩\langle n_{3d}\rangle is the expectation value of the number of 3​d3d electrons. The effective spin expectation value, ⟨Seff⟩=⟨Sz⟩+72​⟨Tz⟩\langle S_{\rm eff}\rangle=\langle S_{z}\rangle+\frac{7}{2}\langle T_{z}\rangle, which includes the magnetic dipole operator contribution ⟨Tz⟩\langle T_{z}\rangle, is evaluated as

⟨Seff⟩\displaystyle\langle S_{\rm eff}\rangle =−3​∫L3XMCD​𝑑E−2​∫L2XMCD​𝑑E∫L3+L2XAS​𝑑E​(10−⟨n3​d⟩)\displaystyle=-\frac{3\int_{L_{3}}\mathrm{XMCD}\penalty\ dE-2\int_{L_{2}}\mathrm{XMCD}\penalty\ dE}{\int_{L_{3}+L_{2}}\mathrm{XAS}\penalty\ dE}(10-\langle n_{3d}\rangle)
=−(3​p−2​q)​(10−⟨n3​d⟩)r,\displaystyle=-\frac{(3p-2q)(10-\langle n_{3d}\rangle)}{r}, (3)

where pp denotes the integrated XMCD intensity over the L3L_{3} edge. The magnetic dipole operator ⟨Tz⟩\langle T_{z}\rangle measures the anisotropy of the spin density distribution – it vanishes for spherical charge distributions, and should remain small but non-zero in a weakly trigonally distorted environment.

Assuming an ionic, high-spin Co2+ 3​d73d^{7} electronic configuration without any mixed-valence effects, corresponding to ⟨n3​d⟩=7\langle n_{3d}\rangle=7, and using the pp, qq, and rr values extracted from the integration curves shown in Fig. 2(a,b), the sum-rules analysis yields ⟨Lz⟩=0.034​(7)\langle L_{z}\rangle=0.034(7) and ⟨Seff⟩=0.024​(5)\langle S_{\rm eff}\rangle=0.024(5), corresponding to ⟨Lz⟩/⟨Seff⟩=1.38​(15)\langle L_{z}\rangle/\langle S_{\rm eff}\rangle=1.38(15). The quoted uncertainties account for the systematic sensitivity of the sum-rule analysis to the spectral processing parameters, as detailed in the SM [1].

The corresponding orbital moment is mL=0.034​(7)​μBm_{L}=0.034(7)\,\mu_{\rm B}. For high-spin Co2+, the effective-spin sum rule is subject to a correction associated with L3L_{3}–L2L_{2} edge mixing and multiplet effects [44]. Using the corresponding correction factor CS≃1.08C_{S}\simeq 1.08 gives mSeffcorr=0.052​(11)​μBm_{S_{\rm eff}}^{\rm corr}=0.052(11)\,\mu_{\rm B} and mL/mSeffcorr=0.64​(7)m_{L}/m_{S_{\rm eff}}^{\rm corr}=0.64(7). This sizable orbital-to-effective-spin moment ratio is comparable to values reported experimentally for other high-spin Co2+ compounds [40, 9, 20].

The crystal-field multiplet calculations provide an independent comparison with the orbital and spin contributions obtained from the XMCD sum rules. The relevant expectation values were thermally averaged over the calculated states at T=300T=300 K and μ0​H=6\mu_{0}H=6 T. In the OhO_{h} limit, the calculation gives ⟨Lz⟩/⟨Sz⟩=1.055\langle L_{z}\rangle/\langle S_{z}\rangle=1.055 and ⟨Lz⟩/⟨Seff⟩=1.096\langle L_{z}\rangle/\langle S_{\rm eff}\rangle=1.096. Systematic variation of the trigonal crystal-field parameters shows that the orbital and effective-spin contributions remain of comparable magnitude throughout the crystal-field regime compatible with the experimental spectra, while ⟨Tz⟩\langle T_{z}\rangle remains small. The complete evolution of these quantities with DσD_{\sigma} and DτD_{\tau} is presented in the SM [1].

For a direct comparison, vibrating sample magnetometry (VSM) measurements on an oriented crystal of NaCdCo2F7 were performed in the Physical Property Measurement System (PPMS14). The magnetic moment measured at 300 K and μ0​H=6\mu_{0}H=6 T with field applied along the cubic [100] direction was found to be mVSM300​K,6​T=0.092​μBm^{\rm 300K,6T}_{\rm VSM}=0.092\penalty\ \mu_{\rm B}. The corrected XMCD-derived moment, mXMCD300​K,6​T=mL+mSeffcorr≃0.086​(13)​μBm_{\rm XMCD}^{\rm 300K,6T}=m_{L}+m_{S_{\rm eff}}^{\rm corr}\simeq 0.086(13)\penalty\ \mu_{\rm B}, is in good agreement with the bulk magnetization value. The spin sum rule probes the effective quantity ⟨Seff⟩=⟨Sz⟩+72​⟨Tz⟩\langle S_{\rm eff}\rangle=\langle S_{z}\rangle+\frac{7}{2}\langle T_{z}\rangle rather than the pure spin contribution ⟨Sz⟩\langle S_{z}\rangle. The crystal-field multiplet calculations show that ⟨Tz⟩\langle T_{z}\rangle remains small in the OhO_{h} and weakly trigonal regimes compatible with the experimental spectra, indicating only a modest magnetic-dipole contribution. Additional systematic uncertainty may arise from the surface-sensitive TEY detection mode, including saturation effects and possible differences between the surface and bulk magnetic response. Further details and comparison of the experimental and calculated moment projections are provided in the SM [1].

The enhanced mL/mSeffcorr=0.64​(7)m_{L}/m_{S_{\rm eff}}^{\rm corr}=0.64(7) ratio provides clear evidence that the orbital moment of Co2+ remains substantially unquenched in NaCdCo2F7, highlighting the importance of SOC in its low-energy magnetic degrees of freedom. Such spin-orbit-entangled Co2+ moments can exhibit strongly anisotropic local magnetic properties and are consistent with the local XY-type anisotropy previously established in the isostructural NaA′′A^{\prime\prime}Co2F7 (A′′A^{\prime\prime} = Ca, Sr) pyrochlores [53, 52].

We note that due to the insulating nature of NaCdCo2F7, TEY measurements at lower temperatures (10 K and 2 K) suffered from a significantly reduced signal-to-noise ratio due to sample charging effects and reduced electron yield, and were not considered for analysis. Alternative detection modes, including Co L​αL\alpha partial electron yield (PEY) or the O K​αK\alpha inverse partial fluorescence yield (iPFY) mode did not provide sufficient signal quality for quantitative XMCD analysis. Consequently, the determination of orbital and spin magnetic moment was restricted to the (300 K, 6 T) TEY dataset. Under these conditions the paramagnetic moment of the highly frustrated pyrochlore Co2+ antiferromagnet remains very low and far from saturation, which limits the quantitative accuracy of the XMCD sum-rules analysis.

III.3 Muon spin relaxation spectroscopy

Ground-state spin dynamics were probed by means of muon spin relaxation (μ\muSR) spectroscopy. Zero-field (ZF) measurements, summarized in Fig. 3(a), reveal oscillations stemming from the F-–μ+\mu^{+}–F- state, as previously seen in the isostructural NaCdCu2F7 and NaCaNi2F7 fluoride pyrochlores [33, 10] and other fluoride materials [8, 68]. At 50 K, the dipolar oscillations are most pronounced and in the cubic lattice, the ZF F-μ\mu-F function GF−μ−F​(t)G_{F-\mu-F}(t) has the form [8]

GF−μ−F(t)=16[\displaystyle G_{\rm F-\mu-F}(t)=\frac{1}{6}\Big[\; 3+cos⁡(3​ωd​t+ϕ)\displaystyle 3+\cos(\sqrt{3}\,\omega_{d}t+\phi)
+(1−13)​cos⁡(3−32​ωd​t+ϕ)\displaystyle+\left(1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right)\cos\!\left(\frac{3-\sqrt{3}}{2}\,\omega_{d}t+\phi\right)
+(1+13)cos(3+32ωdt+ϕ)],\displaystyle+\left(1+\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right)\cos\!\left(\frac{3+\sqrt{3}}{2}\,\omega_{d}t+\phi\right)\Big], (4)

where ϕ\phi is a small phase shift to account for a finite time until thermalization of muons in the stopping site, and ωd\omega_{d} is the dipolar interaction frequency.

As we cool down and approach the spin-glass-like transition, seen by DC and AC susceptibility measurements around Tf=4T_{f}=4 K [32], the electronic fluctuations progressively slow down and enter the muon time window, eventually washing out the F-–μ+\mu^{+}–F- oscillations by the emergence of a broad quasi-static electronic field distribution due to spin freezing. These increasing electronic fluctuations manifest as an exponential damping of the F-–μ+\mu^{+}–F- signal, GF−μ−F​(t)​e−λZF​tG_{\rm F-\mu-F}(t)e^{-\lambda_{\rm ZF}t}.

We note that even at the lowest temperatures, there is an absence of the characteristic minimum then a recovery to a 13\frac{1}{3}-tail at longer times, as expected for a canonical static spin-glass state, following the Kubo-Toyabe relaxation [38]. Instead, a fully monotonic decay of asymmetry is observed at the lowest temperatures, indicating that the local fields are not fully static on the muon timescale, suggesting persistent spin dynamics. The observation of continued dynamics, in an otherwise spin-glass-like state motivates the use of a Dynamic Gaussian Kubo–Toyabe (DGKT) function [26]. This function incorporates an additional relaxation pathway, that takes into account a persistent fluctuating distribution of local magnetic fields. At high fluctuation rate, ν\nu, this collapses to an exponential decay, whilst vanishing fluctuation rate leaves the static Kubo-Toyabe function. At intermediate rates, these fluctuations increasingly wash out the features of the Kubo-Toyabe function, relaxing the expected 13\frac{1}{3}-tail:

GDGKT​(t)=gz​(t)​e−ν​t+ν​∫0tgz​(τ)​e−ν​τ​GDGKT​(t−τ)​𝑑τ.G_{\rm DGKT}(t)=g_{\rm z}(t)e^{-\nu t}+\nu\int_{0}^{t}g_{\rm z}(\tau)e^{-\nu\tau}G_{\rm DGKT}(t-\tau)d\tau. (5)

Here, ν\nu corresponds to the fluctuation rate of the local fields, and gz​(t)g_{z}(t) in zero field has the form of a static Kubo-Toyabe function with a quasi-static field distribution ΔZF\Delta_{\rm ZF}:

gz​(t,H=0)=[13+23​(1−ΔZF2​t2)​e−12​ΔZF2​t2].g_{\rm z}(t,H=0)=\left[\frac{1}{3}+\frac{2}{3}(1-\Delta_{\rm ZF}^{2}t^{2})e^{-\frac{1}{2}\Delta_{\rm ZF}^{2}t^{2}}\right]. (6)

The full temperature-dependence of the ZF relaxation of asymmetry was found to be best described by a function that combines both the DGKT, and the damped F-–μ+\mu^{+}–F- oscillations as discrete contributions:

AZF​(t)=\displaystyle A_{\rm ZF}(t)= Aexp​GF−μ−F​(t)​e−λZF​t\displaystyle A_{\rm exp}G_{\rm F-\mu-F}(t)e^{-\lambda_{\rm ZF}t}
+ADGKT​GDGKT​(t,ΔZF,νZF,H=0)+Abase\displaystyle+A_{\rm DGKT}G_{\mathrm{DGKT}}(t,\Delta_{\rm ZF},\nu_{\rm ZF},H=0)+A_{\rm base} (7)

where Aexp,ADGKTA_{\rm exp},A_{\rm DGKT} are the relaxing amplitudes of these components, λZF\lambda_{\rm ZF} is the zero-field muon relaxation rate, and AbaseA_{\rm base} is a flat baseline corresponding to non-relaxing muons stopping outside the sample.

The need for two contributions implies two distinct stopping sites for the muons, which has been seen previously in these materials, and justified with DFT-based muon implantation calculations [10].

The fits are shown in Fig. 3(a) as dashed lines, and the fitted parameters are summarized in Fig. 3(b). An initial fit was performed at 50 K, where the F-μ\mu-F oscillations are best defined, yielding a phase shift of ϕ=−0.14​(3)\phi=-0.14(3) and the dipolar frequency ωd/2​π=0.2146​(16)\omega_{d}/2\pi=0.2146(16) MHz, corresponding to a μ−\mu-F separation rμ−F=(μ0​γμ​γF​ℏ/4​π​ωd)13=1.19​(1)r_{\mu-F}=(\mu_{0}\gamma_{\mu}\gamma_{F}\hbar/4\pi\omega_{d})^{\frac{1}{3}}=1.19(1) Å, or equivalently the F-μ\mu-F bond length 2​rμ−F=2.38​(2)2r_{\mu-F}=2.38(2) Å. Here, γμ/2​π=135.539\gamma_{\mu}/2\pi=135.539 MHz/T and γF/2​π=40.053\gamma_{F}/2\pi=40.053 MHz/T are the muon and fluorine gyromagnetic ratios, respectively. These parameters were then fixed and a sequential fit between 1.7−501.7-50 K was performed. The flat baseline AbaseA_{\rm base} and the quasi-static field distribution ΔZF\Delta_{\rm ZF} proved to be mostly temperature-independent, and were subsequently fixed to Abase=3.2%A_{\rm base}=3.2\penalty\ \% and ΔZF=0.3\Delta_{\rm ZF}=0.3 MHz, corresponding to a field distribution of δ​Hloc=ΔZF/γμ=22.1\delta H_{\rm loc}=\Delta_{\rm ZF}/\gamma_{\mu}=22.1 G. The temperature dependence of the zero-field relaxation rate λZF\lambda_{\rm ZF}, and the field fluctuation rate νZF\nu_{\rm ZF}, can be seen in Fig. 3(b). We note a steep increase in λZF\lambda_{\rm ZF} below 10 K, reaching up to ∼5\sim\!5 MHz. This is evidently due to the fact that the extremely fast relaxation of asymmetry at short times, caused by the large Co2+ magnetic moment of μeff=5.4​μB\mu_{\rm eff}=5.4\penalty\ \mu_{\rm B}, cannot be fully resolved with the limited time resolution of the MUSR pulsed-source instrument. This also explains the loss of relaxing amplitude AexpA_{\rm exp}, seen in the inset of Fig. 3(b), with decreasing temperature. The fluctuation rate νZF\nu_{\rm ZF} shows a peak centered around 6 K, reaching νZF∼0.4\nu_{\rm ZF}\sim 0.4 MHz, indicating increased dynamics during the spin-freezing process.

To compare the dynamics below and above the spin-freezing transition expected at Tf=4T_{f}=4 K, we measured the field dependence of muon asymmetry at T=1.7T=1.7 and 8 K, seen in Fig. 4. The rapid loss of asymmetry at t<0.5​μt<0.5\penalty\ \mus is evident at 1.7 K, followed by a slow relaxation which saturates at 13 % in an applied field of just μ0​HLF=\mu_{0}H_{\rm LF}= 100 G. This suggests the presence of quasi-static internal fields with a dynamically fluctuating component. At 8 K, above TfT_{f}, we see an exponential relaxation confirming a fast-fluctuating paramagnetic regime.

To quantitatively describe the spin dynamics in this system, the interaction within the F-μ\mu-F state could be decoupled using a 50 G longitudinal field (LF), leaving the DGKT response dominated by electronic fluctuations. The LF 50 G temperature dependence can be seen in Fig. 5(a). Again, we note a rapid depolarization at t<0.5​μt<0.5\penalty\ \mus, followed by a slow relaxation of asymmetry, with a small residual F-μ\mu-F hump around 1 μ\mus visible at high temperatures. The data were fitted using the function

ALF​(t)=ADGKT​GDGKT​(t,ΔLF,νLF,HLF=50​G)+AbaseA_{\rm LF}(t)=A_{\rm DGKT}G_{\rm DGKT}(t,\Delta_{\rm LF},\nu_{\rm LF},H_{\mathrm{LF}}=50\penalty\ \mathrm{G})+A_{\rm base} (8)

where GDGKT​(t,ΔLF,νLF,HLF=50​G)G_{\rm DGKT}(t,\Delta_{\rm LF},\nu_{\rm LF},H_{\mathrm{LF}}=50\penalty\ \mathrm{G}) is defined the same way as in Equation 7, but uses a field-dependent gz​(t,HLF)g_{z}(t,H_{\rm LF}) inside an applied field μ0​HLF=ω0/(2​π​γμ)\mu_{0}H_{\rm LF}=\omega_{0}/(2\pi\gamma_{\mu}) as

gz(t,HLF)=[1\displaystyle g_{z}(t,H_{\rm LF})=\Big[1 −2​Δ2ω02​(1−cos⁡(ω0​t)​e−12​ΔLF2​t2)\displaystyle-2\frac{\Delta^{2}}{\omega_{0}^{2}}\left(1-\cos(\omega_{0}t)e^{-\frac{1}{2}\Delta_{\rm LF}^{2}t^{2}}\right)
+2Δ4ω04ω0∫0tsin(ω0τ)e−12​ΔLF2​τ2dτ].\displaystyle+2\frac{\Delta^{4}}{\omega_{0}^{4}}\omega_{0}\int_{0}^{t}\sin(\omega_{0}\tau)e^{-\frac{1}{2}\Delta_{\rm LF}^{2}\tau^{2}}d\tau\Big]. (9)

The fits can be seen in Fig. 5(a) as dashed lines. The flat background remained largely temperature-independent, and was fixed to Abase=11.4%A_{\rm base}=11.4\%, now corresponding to muons stopping outside the sample as well as muons in quasi-static local field environments easily repolarized by the weak longitudinal field. The sequentially-fitted parameters are summarized in Fig. 5(b). We observe a peak in the quasi-static field distribution ΔLF\Delta_{\rm LF} centered around 4 K, as well as a peak in the fluctuation rate νLF\nu_{\rm LF} at 6 K, consistent with a critical slowing down of spin fluctuations near the freezing transition. The maximum value of ΔLF=2.70​(7)\Delta_{\rm LF}=2.70(7) MHz corresponds to the quasi-static local field distribution δ​Hloc=ΔLF/γμ=199​(5)\delta H_{\rm loc}=\Delta_{\rm LF}/\gamma_{\mu}=199(5) G. The relaxing amplitude, seen in the inset of Fig. 5(b), drops similarly as in the ZF measurement, hinting at the difficulty of fitting the unresolved fast-relaxing part of asymmetry below t<0.5​μt<0.5\penalty\ \mus. Together, these results indicate a partially frozen magnetic state with persistent low-temperature spin dynamics, rather than a canonical static spin glass. Similar partial freezing and continued spin dynamics was seen in the isostructural analogue NaCaNi2F7 [10, 46].

III.4 Nuclear magnetic resonance

Temperature-dependent 23Na NMR spectra measured between 1.7−201.7-20 K on an oriented single crystal in an applied field μ0​H0=2.21331\mu_{0}H_{0}=2.21331 T parallel to the [100] direction are shown in Fig. 6(a). The spectra consist of three sets of resonance lines: (i) the intrinsic 23Na signal from the sample (I=3/2I=3/2, γNa/2​π=11.2625\gamma_{\rm Na}/2\pi=11.2625 MHz/T, 100 % abundance), (ii) an extrinsic 27Al signal (I=5/2I=5/2, γAl/2​π=11.094\gamma_{\rm Al}/2\pi=11.094 MHz/T, 100 % abundance) originating from a small piece of pure Al foil mounted adjacent to the sample as a field marker, and (iii) an extrinsic 63Cu signal (I=3/2I=3/2, γCu/2​π=11.285\gamma_{\rm Cu}/2\pi=11.285 MHz/T, 69.09 % abundance) arising from a copper contact pad on the sample holder. The weak 63Cu signal is too small to be resolved at higher temperatures and becomes discernible only below ∼\sim5 K in the present spectra.

In the pyrochlore structure, the 23Na nuclei occupy the axially symmetric AA site (point symmetry 3¯​m\overline{3}m) where they are randomly distributed with Cd2+ ions with equal probability [32]. This site symmetry results in an axially symmetric electric field gradient (EFG) with the asymmetry parameter η=0\eta=0, whose principal axis is oriented along the local ⟨111⟩\langle 111\rangle directions. For an applied field along H0|[100]H_{0}\parallel[100], the angle between the field and the EFG principal axis corresponds to the magic angle θ=54.7​°\theta=54.7\degree, causing the quadrupolar shift as a first-order perturbation proportional to [3​cos2⁡(θ)−1][3\cos^{2}(\theta)-1] to vanish. As a result, only a single central transition is observed, consistent with the previous 23Na NMR study on the isostructural NaCaCo2F7 [56].

Correspondingly, the spectra seen in Fig, 6(a) were decomposed into three Gaussian components. The positions and linewidths of the extrinsic 27Al and 63Cu signals were fixed to their well-defined values at 1.7 K, while their amplitudes and the parameters of the 23Na line were allowed to vary. At high temperatures (10–20 K), the 23Na line is relatively narrow, consistent with a paramagnetic state characterized by fast electronic spin fluctuations that average out local hyperfine fields. Upon cooling below 10 K, we observe a continual broadening of the 23Na central transition peak, reflecting a development of a spatially inhomogeneous distribution of quasi-static internal fields at the 23Na site. This broad field distribution reflects the spatial randomness of the local magnetic environment, as expected when Co2+ spin dynamics slow down and short-range magnetic correlations become increasingly inhomogeneous. In such a regime, the same magnetic randomness is also expected to enhance transverse relaxation through slowly fluctuating local fields and a distribution of local relaxation rates. Therefore, the strong reduction of the observable 23Na signal intensity below ∼\sim5 K can be naturally understood as a wipeout-like effect, in which a fraction of the nuclei relaxes too rapidly in the transverse channel for the spin echo to be detected within the experimental time window. At 1.7 K, the fitted full width at half maximum (FWHM) of the 23Na resonance is Δ​νNa=2.4​(1)\Delta\nu_{\rm Na}=2.4(1) MHz, corresponding to a local field distribution δ​Hloc=Δ​νNa/γNa=2130​(90)\delta H_{\rm loc}=\Delta\nu_{\rm Na}/\gamma_{\rm Na}=2130(90) G at the 23Na site.

The nuclear spin-lattice relaxation rate 1/T11/T_{1} was determined at each temperature by measuring the recovery of the nuclear magnetization at the position of the resonance peak. The recovery curves were fitted using a stretched exponential function:

M⁡(∞)−M⁡(t)M⁡(∞)\displaystyle\frac{M(\infty)-M(t)}{M(\infty)} =a​exp⁡{−(t/T1)β}.\displaystyle=a\exp\{-\left(t/T_{1}\right)^{\beta}\}. (10)

Here, M⁡(t)M(t) is the nuclear magnetization at time tt after the saturation pulse and M⁡(∞)M(\infty) its equilibrium value. The coefficient aa accounts for the inversion or saturation efficiency of the nuclear magnetization produced by the pulse sequence. When the stretching exponent β=1\beta=1, there is a single uniform relaxation time, and when β<1\beta<1 this indicates a distribution of inhomogeneous dynamics.

The nuclear spin-lattice relaxation rate 1/T11/T_{1}, shown on the left axis in Fig. 6(b), exhibits approximately a 10-fold increase upon cooling from 60 K to 8 K, followed by an abrupt drop by four orders of magnitude upon cooling to 3 K. This is in contrast to canonical spin glasses, where a peak in 1/T11/T_{1} is typically observed due to critical slowing down. The quantity 1/T1​T1/T_{1}T, which probes the low-frequency limit of the momentum q-averaged dynamical spin susceptibility as

(1/T1​T)∼∑q|Aq|2​(χ′′​(q,ω0)/ω0)ω0→0(1/T_{1}T)\sim\sum\limits_{\textbf{q}}|A_{\textbf{q}}|^{2}\left(\chi^{\prime\prime}(\textbf{q},\omega_{0})/\omega_{0}\right)_{\omega_{0}\rightarrow 0} (11)

shows an approximately Curie-like behavior with a maximum at 7 K. The rapid decrease below this temperature suggests that the dominant spectral weight of the spin fluctuations shifts to frequencies lower than the NMR window (<∼107<\penalty\ \sim\!10^{7} Hz) as the system enters the freezing regime. It should be noted, however, that in this temperature range the observable 23Na signal intensity is also strongly reduced. Therefore, the measured 1/T11/T_{1} should be regarded as an effective relaxation rate of the remaining observable NMR component, while nuclei experiencing extremely fast transverse relaxation may be lost from the detected echo signal.

In contrast to the isostructural NaCaCo2F7 [56], where a well-defined Bloembergen–Purcell–Pound (BPP) peak in 1/T1​(T)1/T_{1}(T) was observed [7] as

1/T1​(T)=γ2​h02​τC​(T)1+ω02​τC​(T)2,1/T_{1}(T)=\gamma^{2}h_{0}^{2}\frac{\tau_{C}(T)}{1+\omega_{0}^{2}\tau_{C}(T)^{2}}, (12)

associated with thermally activated low-energy spin fluctuations with a correlation time τC​(T)=τ0​exp⁡(Ea/T)\tau_{C}(T)=\tau_{0}\exp(E_{a}/T), no such peak is detected in NaCdCo2F7. While a BPP maximum typically arises when a single characteristic correlation time 1/τC​(T)1/\tau_{C}(T) crosses the NMR resonance frequency ω0\omega_{0}, our data indicate a broad distribution of fluctuation rates, as evidenced by the strongly reduced stretching exponent β∼0.2\beta\sim 0.2 below 7 K, as seen in the inset of Fig. 6(b). In this situation, different regions of the sample satisfy the BPP condition at different temperatures, leading to a broadening or masking of the expected peak. The absence of a sharp BPP maximum therefore points to a highly inhomogeneous slowing down of spin dynamics, consistent with strong bond disorder on the pyrochlore lattice. This picture is also compatible with μ\muSR results suggesting persistent low-temperature spin fluctuations.

IV Discussion

The combined high-field magnetization and XMCD results establish NaCdCo2F7 as a spin-orbit-entangled pyrochlore antiferromagnet whose low-energy magnetic properties are governed by a well-isolated Jeff=12J_{\rm eff}=\frac{1}{2} Kramers doublet. Although direct determination of the crystal-field level scheme by INS is prohibited by the strong neutron absorption of natural Cd, the large effective gg factor of 6.56 extracted from high-field magnetization, together with the substantial unquenched orbital contribution revealed by XMCD, mL/mSeffcorr=0.64​(7)m_{L}/m_{S_{\rm eff}}^{\rm corr}=0.64(7), provide strong evidence for the importance of SOC in the Co2+ ground state. These observations are fully consistent with previous studies of the isostructural NaCaCo2F7 and NaSrCo2F7 pyrochlores, where a strongly anisotropic local X​YXY-type gg tensor and a spin-orbit-entangled Jeff=12J_{\rm eff}=\frac{1}{2} Kramers doublet have been established by INS experiments.

The Co L2,3L_{2,3} XAS spectra are found to be consistent with a predominantly octahedral (OhO_{h}) crystal field, while remaining compatible with weak trigonal perturbations. This observation is consistent with recent RIXS measurements on NaCaNi2F7, which demonstrated that the local transition-metal electronic structure of fluoride pyrochlores is remarkably robust against AA-site disorder and remains close to ideal octahedral symmetry despite the presence of significant Na/Ca site mixing [17]. The dominant consequence of the cationic AA-site mixing therefore does not seem to lie in changing the local electronic structure, but rather in producing randomness in the magnetic exchange pathways, resulting in bond disorder on the pyrochlore lattice.

The low-temperature μ\muSR and 23Na NMR results provide complementary evidence for how this bond disorder manifests itself in the spin dynamics. Both techniques reveal a progressive slowing down of fluctuations below approximately 10 K, consistent with the development of increasingly inhomogeneous short-range correlations. In μ\muSR, this appears as a strong enhancement of the muon relaxation rate and the emergence of quasi-static and fluctuating local fields. Meanwhile, NMR detects a pronounced broadening of the 23Na line and a loss of intensity in a wipeout-like effect, together with a stretched-exponential relaxation of nuclear magnetization characterized by a strongly suppressed stretching exponent β∼0.2\beta\sim 0.2 below 8 K. The absence of a conventional static Kubo–Toyabe recovery in μ\muSR, together with the suppression of a well-defined BPP peak in 1/T1​(T)1/T_{1}(T) previously seen in NaCaCo2F7 [56], indicate that spin freezing proceeds through a broad distribution of local fluctuation rates rather than through a uniform slowing down process. Such behavior points to a highly inhomogeneous magnetic state arising from bond disorder.

Importantly, the low-temperature state deviates significantly from a canonical spin glass. While DC and AC susceptibility measurements identify a bulk spin-glass-like transition at Tf∼4T_{f}\sim 4 K [32], both local-probe techniques, μ\muSR and 23Na NMR, reveal a more gradual slowing down of spin fluctuations beginning already below ∼8\sim 8 K, indicating that the freezing process develops continuously over an extended temperature range. Despite the apparent spin freezing, persistent low-temperature spin dynamics remain clearly visible on the muon timescale. Such coexistence of quasi-static and fluctuating spin components closely resembles the behavior reported for the isostructural S=1S=1 Heisenberg pyrochlore antiferromagnet NaCaNi2F7 [10], where frozen magnetism similarly coexists with continued dynamics at low temperature. The present results therefore support an emerging picture in which bond-disordered NaA′′​M2A^{\prime\prime}M_{2}F7 (A′′A^{\prime\prime} = Ca, Sr, Cd; MM = Co, Ni, Mn, Fe) fluoride pyrochlores frequently realize unconventional spin-glass-like states, where geometric frustration inhibits complete static freezing even well below TfT_{f}.

A striking comparison with NaCdCu2F7 arises [33], as two fluoride pyrochlores with comparable bond disorder realize fundamentally different ground states: a random-singlet state in the Heisenberg S=12S=\frac{1}{2} Cu2+ system, and an unconventional spin-glass-like state in the spin-orbit-entangled Jeff=12J_{\rm eff}=\frac{1}{2} Co2+ analogue. While NaCdCu2F7 exhibits a disorder-driven random-singlet state characterized by power-law scaling of bulk and local-probe thermodynamic quantities, with data collapse onto universal curves and the absence of bulk spin freezing, NaCdCo2F7 develops a partially-frozen spin-glass-like state with persistent low-temperature spin dynamics. This contrast is particularly remarkable because both materials host (effective) spin-12\frac{1}{2} magnetic moments on the geometrically frustrated pyrochlore lattice, where strong quantum fluctuations would naively be expected to suppress magnetic freezing. However, XMCD measurements demonstrate that the Co2+ moments retain a substantial unquenched orbital contribution, highlighting the importance of strong spin-orbit coupling. Together with the local XY anisotropy and anisotropic exchange interactions established in the isostructural NaA′′A^{\prime\prime}Co2F7 (A′′=A^{\prime\prime}= Ca, Sr) analogues, these ingredients appear to fundamentally alter the response to bond disorder and favor glassy freezing over random-singlet formation. This comparison highlights spin-orbit coupling as a key tuning parameter governing the fate of bond-disordered pyrochlore antiferromagnets.

V Conclusions

We have investigated the magnetic ground state of the bond-disordered pyrochlore antiferromagnet NaCdCo2F7 using high-field magnetization, Co L2,3L_{2,3}-edge XAS/XMCD, μ\muSR, and 23Na NMR measurements. High-field magnetization supports the presence of a well-isolated spin-orbit-entangled Jeff=12J_{\rm eff}=\frac{1}{2} ground-state Kramers doublet characterized by a large effective gg factor and strong antiferromagnetic interactions. XMCD measurements reveal a substantial unquenched orbital contribution to the Co2+ magnetic moment, consistent with strong SOC and the emergence of local X​YXY-type single-ion anisotropy seen in the isostructural NaA′′A^{\prime\prime}Co2F7 (A′′A^{\prime\prime} = Ca, Sr) analogues. Both μ\muSR and NMR measurements demonstrate a progressive slowing down of spin fluctuations below approximately 10 K, culminating in a partially frozen magnetic state. However, persistent low-temperature spin dynamics are observed by μ\muSR, indicating that the frozen state deviates from a conventional static spin glass. A comparison with the isostructural S=12S=\frac{1}{2} Heisenberg antiferromagnet NaCdCu2F7 with a random singlet ground state reveals a fundamentally different response of spin-orbit-entangled Jeff=12J_{\rm eff}=\frac{1}{2} Co2+ moments to bond disorder on the pyrochlore lattice. Together, these results establish NaCdCo2F7 as a disorder-driven spin-glass-like pyrochlore exhibiting persistent low-temperature dynamics arising from strongly spin-orbit-coupled Jeff=12J_{\rm eff}=\frac{1}{2} moments.

I Co2+ L2,3L_{2,3}-edge XAS & XMCD simulations

I.1 Sensitivity to the trigonal crystal field

To examine the sensitivity of the calculated Co L2,3L_{2,3}-edge XAS and XMCD spectra to a weak trigonal distortion of the octahedral crystal field, additional crystal-field multiplet calculations were performed using Crispy [51], a graphical interface to the Quanty computational framework [42]. These calculations are not treated as fits to the experimental spectra. Rather, the crystal-field parameters are varied systematically and the resulting spectra are compared with experiment to identify regimes consistent with the observed spectral line shapes. The resulting crystal-field parameters should therefore be regarded as qualitative rather than as a quantitative determination of the crystal-field splitting.

To quantify the agreement between calculated and experimental spectra, in addition to inspection of the spectral line shapes, we define the normalized residual factor

R=[∫E1E2[Iexp​(E)−Icalc​(E)]2​𝑑E∫E1E2[Iexp​(E)]2​𝑑E]1/2,R=\left[\frac{\displaystyle\int_{E_{1}}^{E_{2}}\left[I^{\rm exp}(E)-I^{\rm calc}(E)\right]^{2}\,dE}{\displaystyle\int_{E_{1}}^{E_{2}}\left[I^{\rm exp}(E)\right]^{2}\,dE}\right]^{1/2}, (1)

where Iexp​(E)I^{\rm exp}(E) and Icalc​(E)I^{\rm calc}(E) are the experimental and calculated intensities, respectively, and E1E_{1} and E2E_{2} define the common energy interval. The residual factors were evaluated separately for the XAS and XMCD spectra over the same energy interval for all calculations. Smaller values of RR indicate closer agreement with experiment. Since the model parameters were not optimized by a fitting procedure and experimental uncertainties are not included in Eq. 1, RR is used only as a relative measure for comparing the calculated spectra.

The calculations were performed for the CoL2,32+{}^{2+}L_{2,3} edge in C3​vC_{3v} symmetry at T=300T=300 K and μ0​H=6\mu_{0}H=6 T, corresponding to the experimental conditions. The octahedral crystal-field splitting was fixed at 10​D​q=0.910Dq=0.9 eV, the Slater-integral reduction factors at Fk=0.75F_{k}=0.75 and Gk=0.78G_{k}=0.78, and the spin-orbit coupling scaling factor at ζ=1\zeta=1. The calculated spectra were broadened using Lorentzian and Gaussian functions with full widths at half maximum (FWHM) of 0.430.43 eV and 0.100.10 eV, respectively. To isolate the effects of the two trigonal crystal-field parameters, DσD_{\sigma} and DτD_{\tau} were varied separately. We first fixed Dτ=0D_{\tau}=0 and varied DσD_{\sigma} from −0.15-0.15 to +0.15+0.15 eV in steps of 0.050.05 eV. For Dσ=Dτ=0D_{\sigma}=D_{\tau}=0, the trigonal contribution vanishes and the calculation reduces to the octahedral OhO_{h} crystal-field limit. Simultaneous variations of DσD_{\sigma} and DτD_{\tau} were not explored, since the purpose of these calculations is to establish the sensitivity of the spectra to trigonal perturbations rather than to determine a unique set of crystal-field parameters.

Figure S1 compares the calculated spectra with the experimental XAS and XMCD data. The XAS line shape is relatively insensitive to weak variations of DσD_{\sigma}, whereas the XMCD response exhibits a stronger dependence on the trigonal crystal field. For XAS, the smallest residual is obtained for Dσ=−0.05D_{\sigma}=-0.05 eV (R=0.0967R=0.0967), compared with R=0.1054R=0.1054 in the OhO_{h} limit and R=0.1020R=0.1020 for Dσ=+0.05D_{\sigma}=+0.05 eV. The differences are small, and all three calculations give similar descriptions of the experimental XAS line shape.

The XMCD residual shows a clearer minimum at the OhO_{h} limit, with R=0.2487R=0.2487 for Dσ=0D_{\sigma}=0, compared with 0.2867 and 0.2664 for Dσ=−0.05D_{\sigma}=-0.05 and +0.05+0.05 eV, respectively. Larger |Dσ||D_{\sigma}| values produce progressively larger XMCD residuals, reaching R=0.3965R=0.3965 and 0.3831 for Dσ=−0.15D_{\sigma}=-0.15 and +0.15+0.15 eV, respectively. The residual analysis therefore favors a crystal field close to the OhO_{h} limit, although weak trigonal perturbations cannot be excluded and a unique value of DσD_{\sigma} cannot be determined from the present results.

The sensitivity to the second trigonal crystal-field parameter was examined independently by fixing Dσ=0D_{\sigma}=0 and varying DτD_{\tau} from −0.010-0.010 to +0.010+0.010 eV. As shown in Fig. S2, even small changes in DτD_{\tau} modify the calculated spectra, particularly the XMCD response. For XAS, the residual decreases from R=0.1054R=0.1054 in the OhO_{h} limit to 0.0933 for Dτ=−0.005D_{\tau}=-0.005 eV and 0.1028 for Dτ=+0.005D_{\tau}=+0.005 eV, with the smallest value, R=0.0887R=0.0887, obtained at both Dτ=−0.010D_{\tau}=-0.010 and +0.010+0.010 eV. The XAS residual therefore does not identify a preferred sign of DτD_{\tau} within the range considered.

For XMCD, negative DτD_{\tau} increases the residual substantially, from R=0.2487R=0.2487 in the OhO_{h} limit to 0.2905 and 0.3624 for Dτ=−0.005D_{\tau}=-0.005 and −0.010-0.010 eV, respectively. Positive DτD_{\tau} produces only small changes, with R=0.2462R=0.2462 and 0.2514 for Dτ=+0.005D_{\tau}=+0.005 and +0.010+0.010 eV, respectively. Although the lowest XMCD residual occurs at Dτ=+0.005D_{\tau}=+0.005 eV, its difference from the OhO_{h} value is marginal and does not provide evidence for a finite DτD_{\tau}.

Taken together, the DσD_{\sigma} and DτD_{\tau} series favor a crystal field close to the OhO_{h} limit. The XMCD residual is minimized at Dσ=0D_{\sigma}=0, while variation of DτD_{\tau} yields no significant improvement over the OhO_{h} result and the XAS and XMCD residuals do not select a common finite DτD_{\tau}. Weak trigonal perturbations remain compatible with the spectra, but their magnitude and sign cannot be determined uniquely from the present results. We therefore retain the OhO_{h} calculation as the minimal description in the main text. Additional constraints from the calculated orbital and spin expectation values are considered below.

I.2 Calculation of orbital and spin expectation values

In addition to the calculated spectral line shapes, the crystal-field multiplet calculations provide the expectation values of the orbital, spin, total angular momentum, and magnetic-dipole operators for each eigenstate. Since the calculations correspond to T=300T=300 K and μ0​H=6\mu_{0}H=6 T, several states are thermally populated. The quantities discussed below are therefore thermal averages over the calculated eigenstates,

⟨A⟩T=∑id​Zi​⟨A⟩i,\langle A\rangle_{T}=\sum_{i}dZ_{i}\langle A\rangle_{i}, (2)

where d​ZidZ_{i} is the normalized Boltzmann weight of the iith state reported by Crispy. The same averaging procedure was applied to ⟨L2⟩\langle L^{2}\rangle, ⟨S2⟩\langle S^{2}\rangle, ⟨J2⟩\langle J^{2}\rangle, ⟨Lz⟩\langle L_{z}\rangle, ⟨Sz⟩\langle S_{z}\rangle, ⟨Jz⟩\langle J_{z}\rangle, ⟨Tz⟩\langle T_{z}\rangle, and ⟨𝐥⋅𝐬⟩\langle\mathbf{l}\cdot\mathbf{s}\rangle, where ⟨𝐥⋅𝐬⟩\langle\mathbf{l}\cdot\mathbf{s}\rangle is the expectation value of the spin–orbit coupling operator.

The effective spin projection relevant to the XMCD spin sum rule is defined as

⟨Seff⟩=⟨Sz⟩+72​⟨Tz⟩.\langle S_{\rm eff}\rangle=\langle S_{z}\rangle+\frac{7}{2}\langle T_{z}\rangle. (3)

Table S1 shows the state-resolved Crispy output for Dσ=Dτ=0D_{\sigma}=D_{\tau}=0, corresponding to the OhO_{h} crystal-field limit, as a representative example of the quantities entering the thermal averages. Crispy denotes projections along the quantization axis by SkS_{k}, LkL_{k}, JkJ_{k}, and TkT_{k}, corresponding here to SzS_{z}, LzL_{z}, JzJ_{z}, and TzT_{z}, respectively.

The same thermal averaging procedure was applied to the calculated output for each value of DσD_{\sigma}, with the resulting quantities summarized in Table S2.

A notable result is that ⟨S2⟩\langle S^{2}\rangle remains nearly constant at 3.74 throughout the investigated DσD_{\sigma} range, close to S⁡(S+1)=3.75S(S+1)=3.75 for S=3/2S=3/2, confirming that the high-spin Co2+ state is preserved. In contrast, ⟨L2⟩\langle L^{2}\rangle, ⟨J2⟩\langle J^{2}\rangle, and ⟨𝐥⋅𝐬⟩\langle\mathbf{l}\cdot\mathbf{s}\rangle vary appreciably with DσD_{\sigma}, reflecting a redistribution of the orbital and spin–orbit character by the trigonal crystal field. In the OhO_{h} limit, ⟨Lz⟩/⟨Seff⟩=1.096\langle L_{z}\rangle/\langle S_{\rm eff}\rangle=1.096, compared with 0.998 and 1.042 for Dσ=−0.05D_{\sigma}=-0.05 and +0.05+0.05 eV, respectively. Thus, throughout the weakly trigonal regime giving the best spectral agreement, the orbital and effective-spin projections remain of comparable magnitude. The corresponding ⟨Tz⟩\langle T_{z}\rangle values are small, indicating only a modest magnetic-dipole contribution.

For comparison, the experimental XMCD sum-rule analysis gives

⟨Lz⟩exp=0.034​(7),⟨Seff⟩exp=0.024​(5),⟨Lz⟩exp⟨Seff⟩exp=1.38​(15).\langle L_{z}\rangle^{\rm exp}=0.034(7),\qquad\langle S_{\rm eff}\rangle^{\rm exp}=0.024(5),\qquad\frac{\langle L_{z}\rangle^{\rm exp}}{\langle S_{\rm eff}\rangle^{\rm exp}}=1.38(15). (4)

The quoted uncertainties represent conservative estimates of the systematic sensitivity to reasonable variations of the spectral processing parameters. The absolute values are primarily sensitive to the linear pre-edge background, whereas the uncertainty of their ratio is dominated by the endpoint of the L3L_{3} dichroic integral pp in the inter-edge region. The nominal analysis uses pp at 788 eV and the total dichroic integral qq at 800 eV. Although the experimental ratio is somewhat larger than the calculated values, both consistently indicate a substantial unquenched orbital contribution.

To compare the expectation values with magnetic moments, we use mL=μB​|⟨Lz⟩|m_{L}=\mu_{\rm B}|\langle L_{z}\rangle| and mSeff=2​μB​|⟨Seff⟩|m_{S_{\rm eff}}=2\mu_{\rm B}|\langle S_{\rm eff}\rangle|. Consequently, ⟨Lz⟩/⟨Seff⟩=1.38​(15)\langle L_{z}\rangle/\langle S_{\rm eff}\rangle=1.38(15) corresponds to mL/mSeff=0.69​(8)m_{L}/m_{S_{\rm eff}}=0.69(8) before any additional correction. For Co2+, the effective-spin sum rule requires a correction for the incomplete separation of the L3L_{3} and L2L_{2} edges and associated core-hole multiplet effects. Following Piamonteze et al. [44], the calculated spin-sum-rule value for high-spin Co2+ (3​d73d^{7}) with atomic spin–orbit coupling and 10​D​q=0.910Dq=0.9 eV is approximately 0.925 of the exact effective-spin expectation value, corresponding to CS≃1/0.925≃1.08C_{S}\simeq 1/0.925\simeq 1.08. A similar correction has previously been applied to high-spin Co2+ compounds [40]. The resulting experimental moments are therefore

mLexp=0.034​(7)​μB,mSeffexp,corr=0.052​(11)​μB,mLexpmSeffexp,corr=0.64​(7).m_{L}^{\rm exp}=0.034(7)\,\mu_{\rm B},\qquad m_{S_{\rm eff}}^{\rm exp,corr}=0.052(11)\,\mu_{\rm B},\qquad\frac{m_{L}^{\rm exp}}{m_{S_{\rm eff}}^{\rm exp,corr}}=0.64(7). (5)

The orbital-to-effective-spin magnetic-moment ratio is therefore large but physically reasonable for high-spin Co2+.

The absolute moment obtained from the single-ion calculation is somewhat larger than the experimental value because the Hamiltonian does not include the strong antiferromagnetic exchange interactions in NaCdCo2F7. In the OhO_{h} limit at 300 K and 6 T, the calculation gives mL=0.0446​μBm_{L}=0.0446\penalty\ \mu_{\rm B} and mSeff=0.0814​μBm_{S_{\rm eff}}=0.0814\penalty\ \mu_{\rm B}, corresponding to a total moment mcalc=0.126​μBm_{\rm calc}=0.126\penalty\ \mu_{\rm B}. As a simple estimate of the effect of antiferromagnetic correlations, the experimentally determined θCW=−108​(1)\theta_{\rm CW}=-108(1) K gives a Curie–Weiss reduction of the susceptibility relative to the noninteracting Curie response by

χCWχC=TT−θCW=300300+108≃0.735.\frac{\chi_{\rm CW}}{\chi_{\rm C}}=\frac{T}{T-\theta_{\rm CW}}=\frac{300}{300+108}\simeq 0.735. (6)

Applying this factor to the calculated total moment gives mcalcCW≃0.735​mcalc≃0.0926,μBm_{\rm calc}^{\rm CW}\simeq 0.735m_{\rm calc}\simeq 0.0926,\mu_{\rm B}, in close agreement with the experimental magnetization measured at the same temperature and field, mVSM300​K,6​T=0.092​μBm_{\rm VSM}^{300{\rm K},6{\rm T}}=0.092\mu_{\rm B}. This comparison is intended only as a simple mean-field estimate, since exchange interactions are not included explicitly in the single-ion calculation.

Taken together, the spectral comparison and calculated expectation values support a predominantly octahedral crystal-field environment with at most a weak trigonal perturbation whose magnitude and sign cannot be uniquely determined from the present data. Both the calculations and XMCD sum-rule analysis consistently establish a substantial unquenched orbital contribution to the Co2+ magnetic moment, supporting the use of the OhO_{h} calculation as the minimal description in the main text.
